title: How to Pray — The Essentials
subtitle: The five daily prayers, step by step from standing to salaam
steps: Before you begin: be in wudu, with a clean body, clothes and place, the awrah covered, and the time of that prayer entered. Then face the qiblah (Qur'an 2:144). The intention (niyyah) is in the heart: settle on which prayer you are praying. The Prophet ﷺ said actions are judged by intentions (Bukhari 1). It is not reported that he spoke the intention aloud.

Stand and say Allahu Akbar, raising the hands to the level of the shoulders (Bukhari 735) or to the ears (Muslim 391). The prayer is entered by the takbir and left by the taslim (Abu Dawud 61, hasan sahih per al-Albani). Then place the right hand over the left (Bukhari 740: the people were ordered to place the right hand on the left forearm).

Recite the opening supplication (thana') if you know it, seek refuge in Allah and say Bismillah, then Surah al-Fatihah: the Prophet ﷺ said the prayer of one who does not recite it is invalid (Bukhari 756). Say Amin after it (Bukhari 780). In the first two rak'ahs add another surah or some verses; in the last two of a four-rak'ah prayer recite al-Fatihah alone (Bukhari 776).

Aloud or silent: the imam recites aloud in Fajr and in the first two rak'ahs of Maghrib and Isha, and silently in Dhuhr and Asr; the Prophet ﷺ recited aloud in some prayers and quietly in others and his followers do the same (Bukhari 772, 774).

Ruku': say Allahu Akbar and bow, hands on the knees, the back straight and level (Bukhari 828). Say Subhana Rabbiyal-'Azim, the words the Prophet ﷺ said in bowing (Muslim 772). Saying it three times is the usual practice; the report that gives the number is Ibn Majah 888 (sahih per al-Albani; Shuaib al-Arnaut and Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if).
Rise saying Sami'allahu liman hamidah, then Rabbana wa lakal-hamd (Bukhari 735), and stand fully upright until every bone returns to its place (Bukhari 828).

Sujud: say Allahu Akbar and go down on seven parts: the forehead with the nose, both hands, both knees and the toes of both feet (Bukhari 812), the forearms lifted off the ground (Bukhari 828). Say Subhana Rabbiyal-A'la (Muslim 772) and ask Allah for what you need: the servant is nearest to his Lord when he prostrates (Muslim 482). Rise to sit, say Rabbighfir li (Abu Dawud 874, sahih per al-Albani), then prostrate a second time. That is one rak'ah.

Stand for the next rak'ah with a takbir and pray it the same way, without the opening supplication. Fajr is 2 rak'ahs, Dhuhr 4, Asr 4, Maghrib 3, Isha 4. In a prayer of 3 or 4 rak'ahs sit after the second rak'ah for the first tashahhud only, then stand (the hands are raised again: Bukhari 739) and pray the remaining rak'ahs with al-Fatihah alone (Bukhari 776).

The last sitting: the tashahhud (Bukhari 831), then blessings on the Prophet ﷺ (Bukhari 3370), then seek refuge in Allah from four things: the punishment of Hell, the punishment of the grave, the trial of life and death, and the trial of the Dajjal (Muslim 588). Then ask Allah for whatever you wish.
The salaam: say As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah (Abu Dawud 996, sahih per al-Albani), turning the face to the right and then to the left (Muslim 582).

Do every position calmly. The Prophet ﷺ told a man who prayed hurriedly three times: go back and pray, for you have not prayed; then he taught him to be at ease in the bowing, the standing, the prostration and the sitting (Bukhari 757).

If you cannot yet recite al-Fatihah (a new Muslim), the Prophet ﷺ taught a man who could not memorise any Qur'an to say: Subhanallah, wal-hamdu lillah, wa la ilaha illallah, wallahu akbar, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah (Abu Dawud 832, hasan per al-Albani). Say that, and learn al-Fatihah as soon as you can.
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 61 (hasan sahih per al-Albani), 832 (hasan per al-Albani), 874 (sahih per al-Albani), 996 (sahih per al-Albani); Sunan Ibn Majah 888 (sahih per al-Albani)
The differences between the schools stated below are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Fatihah: a pillar (rukn) in the Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools. In the Hanafi school it is wajib (obligatory but not a pillar): the prayer is valid without it but sinful, and it is repeated.
Behind an imam: Hanafi — the follower stays silent, the imam's recitation counts for him. Shafi'i — the follower recites al-Fatihah in every rak'ah. Maliki and Hanbali — the follower is silent in the loud prayers and recites in the silent ones.
Raising the hands: Shafi'i and Hanbali — at the opening takbir, before and after bowing, and when standing for the third rak'ah. Hanafi and (in the relied-upon view) Maliki — at the opening takbir only.
Amin: Shafi'i and Hanbali — aloud in the loud prayers. Hanafi — quietly. Maliki — the imam does not say it aloud; the follower says it after the imam finishes al-Fatihah.
Speaking the intention: required in no school. Shafi'i scholars recommend saying it silently with the takbir; Hanbali scholars discourage it.
Where to put the hands is a separate difference, set out in the Four Schools guide. Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Prayer is a meeting, not a performance: each position carries a meaning — standing in awe, bowing in humility, prostration in nearness (Muslim 482: the nearest a servant comes to his Lord is when he is prostrating, so make much supplication).
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 757 (the man who prayed badly) and Bukhari 828 (Abu Humayd's description of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer) are the two fullest descriptions; the steps above follow them.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Rushing; looking around; reciting the words without knowing what they mean; treating wudu as a formality rather than the threshold of the meeting. Do not wait to be perfect before you pray: pray now, and learn the words as you go.

title: The Five Prayer Times
subtitle: When each prayer begins and ends, and the times when voluntary prayer is forbidden
steps: Allah says: 'Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night and the Qur'an of dawn' (Qur'an 17:78); 'prayer has been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times' (Qur'an 4:103).

Jibril led the Prophet ﷺ twice at the Ka'bah to show the times: Dhuhr when the sun had passed its peak; Asr when the shadow of a thing was equal to it (the first day) and about twice as long (the second day); Maghrib when the sun had set; Isha when the twilight had vanished (the first day) and when a third of the night had gone (the second day); Fajr when dawn appeared and eating is forbidden to the fasting person, and the second day when the land was bright. He said: the time is between these two times (Tirmidhi 149, hasan sahih per al-Albani; isnad hasan per Zubair Ali Zai; Abu Dawud 393, hasan sahih per al-Albani).

The ending of each time: Fajr lasts until the sun begins to rise; Dhuhr until Asr comes; Asr until the sun turns yellow; Maghrib until the twilight has gone; Isha until the middle of the night (Muslim 612).

Pray at the start of the time when you can, and never delay a prayer out of its time without an excuse. Asked which deed is dearest to Allah, the Prophet ﷺ said: to offer the prayers at their early fixed times (Bukhari 527). The missed-prayer guide covers what to do if you miss one.

Times when voluntary prayer is forbidden: Uqbah ibn Amir said the Prophet ﷺ forbade praying, or burying the dead, at three times: when the sun begins to rise until it is fully up, when it stands at its height at midday until it passes the meridian, and when it draws near to setting until it sets (Muslim 831). The Prophet ﷺ also said there is no prayer after Fajr until the sun rises, and none after Asr until the sun sets (Bukhari 586).
A prayer with a cause (a missed prayer, the greeting of the mosque, a funeral prayer) at those times: see the note.
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 393 (hasan sahih per al-Albani)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Asr begins: Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali — when the shadow of a thing equals the thing (plus the midday shadow). Hanafi — when the shadow is twice the thing.
Isha begins: Hanafi (Abu Hanifa) — when the white twilight has gone; the two companions and the other three schools — when the red twilight has gone.
Fajr begins at true dawn in all four schools; there is a modern difference over the sun's angle (see the calculation method in the app).
Prayers with a cause at the forbidden times: Hanafi — not permitted, except Asr of the same day. Shafi'i — permitted (for prayers with a cause). Hanbali — permitted for the funeral prayer and the make-up of an obligatory prayer, not for the greeting of the mosque. Maliki — permitted for missed obligatory prayers and the funeral prayer; voluntary prayers are not.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The five prayers are tied to the sun's path across the sky; the times are fixed by Allah and the calculation in the app follows them.
goDeeper.evidence: The report of Jibril's two days is in the sources; Muslim 612 gives the end of each time.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Praying Fajr after sunrise; praying Dhuhr late into Asr's time without cause; praying voluntary prayers when the sun is rising, at its peak or setting.

title: Praying in Congregation
subtitle: The reward, the rows, and how to follow the imam
steps: The reward: the prayer in congregation is twenty-seven times better than the prayer of one praying alone (Bukhari 645; Muslim 650).
Going to the prayer: when you hear the iqamah, walk with calm and dignity, do not hurry; pray what you catch with the imam and complete what you missed (Bukhari 636).

The rows: straighten your rows, for straightening them is part of perfecting the prayer (Bukhari 723; Muslim 433). Anas said that each of them used to put his shoulder against his neighbour's shoulder and his foot against his neighbour's foot (Bukhari 725).
The best rows for men are the first; for women, the last (Muslim 440).

Following the imam: the imam is appointed to be followed; bow when he bows, rise when he rises, and say Rabbana wa lakal-hamd after he says Sami'allahu liman hamidah (Bukhari 689). Do not go ahead of him.
Who leads: the one who knows the Book of Allah best; if they are equal, the one who knows the Sunnah best (Muslim 673).
Women: do not prevent your women from the mosque (Bukhari 900), though their homes are better for them (Abu Dawud 567, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if).
sources: The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Ruling for men: Hanafi — an emphasised sunnah (some Hanafi scholars say wajib). Maliki — an emphasised sunnah. Shafi'i — a collective obligation (fard kifayah) in the relied-upon view. Hanbali — a personal obligation for men able to attend, though the prayer prayed alone is valid.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The congregation is the visible form of the Muslim community: shoulder to shoulder before Allah.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 645 and Muslim 650 give the reward; Bukhari 636 gives the manner of joining.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Running to the prayer; leaving gaps in the row; standing alone behind the row; going ahead of the imam in movements.

title: Forgetting in Prayer — Sujud as-Sahw
subtitle: The two prostrations that repair a mistake in the prayer
steps: What it is: two extra prostrations made when you forget something in the prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said: I am a human being like you and forget as you forget; so when I forget, remind me (Bukhari 401; Muslim 572).

You forgot the first sitting (the first tashahhud) and stood up: do not go back; finish the prayer, and before the salam say Allahu Akbar and make two prostrations sitting. This is what the Prophet ﷺ did when he stood after two rak'ahs without sitting (Bukhari 1224).

You are in doubt about the number of rak'ahs: the Prophet ﷺ said, cast away the doubt and build on what you are sure of, then make two prostrations before the salam (Muslim 571). In another report he said, aim at what is correct, complete the prayer, then make the two prostrations (Bukhari 401; Muslim 572). The schools differ on which applies; see the note.
You added a rak'ah: the Prophet ﷺ once prayed five rak'ahs of Dhuhr; when told, he made two prostrations (Bukhari 1226; Bukhari 401 and Muslim 572 describe the same).

You finished the prayer early by mistake: the Prophet ﷺ gave the salam after two rak'ahs of a four-rak'ah prayer; when Dhul-Yadayn reminded him, he completed the prayer, gave the salam, then said the takbir and made two prostrations, and again a takbir as he rose (Muslim 573).

How: say Allahu Akbar and prostrate as in a normal prostration, rise with a takbir, prostrate again and rise (Muslim 573); then give the salam, or the tashahhud and the salam, according to your school.
If you left a pillar (a ruku' or a sujud, or al-Fatihah), the two prostrations do not replace it: the rak'ah is not counted and you must do it. The schools agree on this.
sources: The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Ruling: Hanafi — obligatory (wajib) when an obligatory part of the prayer is forgotten or delayed. Maliki and Shafi'i — a sunnah. Hanbali — obligatory when the reason is a forgotten obligatory act, an addition, or a doubt.
Before or after the salam: Hanafi — always after the salam. Shafi'i — always before it. Maliki — before the salam when something was left out, after it when something was added. Hanbali — before the salam where the Prophet ﷺ did so (first tashahhud forgotten; doubt resolved by certainty), after it where he did so (early salam; adding; acting on a firm belief).
Doubt about the number of rak'ahs: Hanafi, Maliki and Hanbali — act on what you think most likely; if neither seems likelier, build on the smaller number. Shafi'i — build on the smaller number.
The narrations differ on whether the Prophet ﷺ prostrated before the salam (Bukhari 1224; Muslim 571) or after it (Bukhari 1226; Muslim 573), which is why the schools differ.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The prayer is a human act and humans forget; the two prostrations are the remedy the Prophet ﷺ prescribed.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 401 and Muslim 571-573 contain every case above.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Going back after fully standing from the first sitting; making the prostrations for a skipped pillar; making them twice.

title: Praying When Travelling, Sick or in Fear
subtitle: Shortening, combining, and praying seated or on a vehicle
steps: Shortening: Allah says: 'And when you travel throughout the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer' (Qur'an 4:101). Yaala ibn Umayyah asked Umar why the people shorten when they are safe; Umar had asked the Prophet ﷺ, who said it is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity (Muslim 686).

Which prayers: only the four-rak'ah prayers (Dhuhr, Asr, Isha) are shortened to two. Fajr and Maghrib are not shortened. The Prophet ﷺ prayed two rak'ahs when travelling, as did Abu Bakr and Umar (Muslim 694; Ibn Majah 1064, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).

How long: the Prophet ﷺ once stayed nineteen days and shortened the prayer (Bukhari 1080); and he stayed twenty days at Tabuk shortening it (Abu Dawud 1235, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if). The schools differ on the limit of the stay and on the distance; see the note.

Combining: Ibn Abbas reported that the Prophet ﷺ combined Dhuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha without fear or travel (Muslim 705); scholars differ on what this meaning allows. Anas said that when the Prophet ﷺ set off before noon he delayed Dhuhr to the time of Asr and combined them, and if the sun passed its peak before he set off he prayed Dhuhr and then rode (Bukhari 1111). The schools differ on this; see the note.

On a mount: the Prophet ﷺ prayed the voluntary prayers on his mount facing whatever direction it took, and prayed witr on it, but not the obligatory prayer; for the obligatory prayer he dismounted and faced the qiblah (Bukhari 1098, 1099). In a car, train or plane, pray the obligatory prayer at its time: on the ground facing the qiblah if you can, otherwise as you are, as far as you are able.
Illness: the Prophet ﷺ told Imran ibn Husayn, who had piles: pray standing; if you cannot, sitting; if you cannot, on your side (Bukhari 1117).
Fear: Allah says: 'And if you fear an enemy, then pray on foot or riding' (Qur'an 2:239).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1235 (sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai: da'if)
Sunan Ibn Majah 1064 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Distance: Hanafi — about 77 km (three days' travel). Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — about 80-83 km (sixteen farsakhs).
Shortening: Hanafi — obligatory. Maliki — a strongly recommended sunnah. Shafi'i and Hanbali — a permission; shortening is better.
How long a stay: Hanafi — intending to stay fifteen days or more makes you a resident. Maliki and Shafi'i — intending to stay four full days. Hanbali — intending to stay more than four days (more than twenty prayers).
Combining while travelling: Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — permitted. Hanafi — only at Arafah and Muzdalifah in Hajj.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Travel, illness and fear do not release you from the prayer; they change its form.
goDeeper.evidence: Muslim 686 gives the charity; Bukhari 1117 gives the stages when ill.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Praying Maghrib as two; combining without a reason; waiting to arrive when a prayer's time is passing.

title: Wudu — The Purifying Wash
subtitle: How the Prophet ﷺ washed for prayer, and what undoes it
steps: Make the intention in the heart (the Prophet ﷺ said actions are by intentions: Bukhari 1), then say Bismillah: he said the wudu of one who does not mention Allah's name is not valid (Abu Dawud 101, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it hasan).
Wash both hands up to the wrists three times (Bukhari 159); the Prophet ﷺ liked to begin with the right side in purification (Bukhari 168).
Rinse the mouth and sniff water into the nose and blow it out, three times (Bukhari 159).
Wash the face three times, from the hairline to the chin and from ear to ear (Qur'an 5:6).
Wash both arms up to and including the elbows, right then left, three times (Qur'an 5:6; Bukhari 159).
Wipe the head once with wet hands (Qur'an 5:6; Bukhari 159), then the ears inside and out (Abu Dawud 121, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai: isnad hasan).
Wash both feet up to and including the ankles, right then left, three times, reaching the heels: the Prophet ﷺ said, save your heels from the Fire (Bukhari 163).
Then say the shahada; the Prophet ﷺ said that the eight gates of Paradise are opened for the one who makes wudu well and says it (Muslim 234).

What breaks wudu in all four schools: anything that leaves the front or back passage (urine, stool, wind: Bukhari 135); madhi, after which one washes the private part and makes wudu (Abu Dawud 207, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if); deep sleep; loss of consciousness. The schools differ on other causes; see the note.
If you are unsure whether you broke wudu, do not leave the prayer on a doubt: the Prophet ﷺ said one should not leave unless he hears a sound or smells something (Bukhari 137).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 101 (sahih per al-Albani), 121 (sahih per al-Albani), 207 (sahih per al-Albani)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Required acts: Hanafi — four: the face, the arms to the elbows, a quarter of the head, the feet. Maliki — the intention, face, arms, the whole head, feet, unbroken sequence, and rubbing the limbs. Shafi'i — six: the intention, face, arms, some part of the head (even a few hairs), feet, and the order. Hanbali — the face (with rinsing the mouth and nose), arms, the whole head and ears, feet, order and sequence; the intention is a condition.
Rinsing mouth and nose: required in the Hanbali school; a sunnah in the other three.
Intention: required in the Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools; in the Hanafi school it is a sunnah that makes wudu rewarded (it is required for tayammum).
Wiping the head: Maliki and Hanbali — all of it; Hanafi — at least a quarter; Shafi'i — some part.
Touching one's own private part: breaks wudu in the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools; not in the Hanafi school; the Maliki ruling depends on the manner of touch and on desire. Skin contact with a woman: breaks it in the Shafi'i school; in the Maliki and Hanbali schools only if with desire; not in the Hanafi school.
Flowing blood or a mouthful of vomit: breaks wudu in the Hanafi school; in the Hanbali school if it is a large amount; not in the Maliki or Shafi'i schools. Eating camel meat breaks wudu in the Hanbali school only.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Wudu is the threshold of the prayer: a small washing that tells the heart a meeting is about to begin.
goDeeper.evidence: Each step carries its own source; the full list is under Sources.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Wasting water; missing the heels and between the toes; leaving dry patches under a watch, a ring or nail varnish that stops water reaching the nail.

title: Ghusl — The Full Purification
subtitle: After janabah and the end of menstruation or post-natal bleeding, and the Friday bath
steps: When it is required: after sexual intercourse (whether or not there is emission: Abu Dawud 214, sahih per al-Albani, which ended the early concession), after emission of semen, and after the end of menstruation and post-natal bleeding. The command: 'and if you are in a state of janabah, then purify yourselves' (Qur'an 5:6).
Make the intention in the heart and say Bismillah.
Wash the hands, then wash the private parts (Bukhari 248).
Make a complete wudu as for prayer (Bukhari 248).

Run the fingers through the roots of the hair and pour three handfuls of water over the head (Bukhari 248). A woman need not undo her plaits (Muslim 330); scholars add: provided the water reaches the roots.

Pour water over the rest of the body, starting with the right side, so that no part is left dry, including the navel and the armpits (Bukhari 248; the Prophet ﷺ liked to start from the right: Bukhari 168).
After menstruation a woman washes away the traces of blood and takes this ghusl; the Prophet ﷺ told the woman who asked to clean the place with a piece of cloth scented with musk (Bukhari 314, 315).

Friday ghusl: the Prophet ﷺ said it is compulsory for every adult male (Bukhari 879) and told whoever comes to the Friday prayer to bathe (Bukhari 877). The four schools treat it as a strongly recommended sunnah; see the note.
sources: The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Rinsing the mouth and nose in ghusl: required in the Hanafi and Hanbali schools; a sunnah in the Maliki and Shafi'i schools. Rubbing the body with the hands: required in the Maliki school.
Emission of semen without desire (for example because of illness): requires ghusl in the Shafi'i school; in the Hanafi, Maliki and Hanbali schools ghusl follows emission with desire. Intercourse and emission with desire require ghusl in all schools.
Ghusl on entering Islam: obligatory in the Maliki and Hanbali schools; recommended in the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools.
Friday ghusl: a strongly recommended sunnah in the four schools; the Zahiri school holds it obligatory.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Ghusl returns the whole body to purity after what makes it impure; the Prophet ﷺ asked for nothing complicated.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 248 is Aisha's description of the Prophet's ﷺ ghusl; the order above is hers.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Leaving the roots of the hair or the navel dry; assuming a shower is enough without the intention; forgetting that ghusl is also required after menstruation ends.

title: Tayammum — The Dry Purification
subtitle: When water is absent, harmful, or out of reach
steps: When it is allowed: when there is no water after looking for it, when water would harm you (illness or a wound), or in danger from extreme cold. The command: 'and do not find water, then seek clean earth and wipe over your faces and hands with it' (Qur'an 5:6; the same ruling is in 4:43). Amr ibn al-As made tayammum on a freezing night for fear of harm, led the prayer, and the Prophet ﷺ did not blame him (Abu Dawud 334, sahih per al-Albani).
Make the intention in the heart and say Bismillah.

Strike the palms once on clean earth (dust, sand or stone). The Prophet ﷺ taught Ammar: it is enough to strike the earth with your hands, then wipe the face and the backs of the hands (Bukhari 341, 343).
Wipe the whole face, then the hands (Qur'an 5:6; Bukhari 343). The schools differ on how far up the arms and whether a second strike is needed; see the note.

Pray with it. The Prophet ﷺ said the earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification (Bukhari 335). Tayammum can be used for the prayers of the time until something breaks it; the schools differ on how many prayers.

Tayammum ends when water becomes available, or when anything that breaks wudu happens. Two men prayed with tayammum, found water within the time, and one repeated the prayer while the other did not; the Prophet ﷺ told the one who did not repeat that he had followed the sunnah (Abu Dawud 338, sahih per al-Albani). The Prophet ﷺ also told a man in janabah who had no water to use clean earth, and later had water poured on him to wash (Bukhari 344).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 334 (sahih per al-Albani), 338 (sahih per al-Albani)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
The strikes and the limit of the arms: Hanafi and Shafi'i — two strikes, the second for the hands and arms up to the elbows. Hanbali — one strike, the face and the palms (to the wrists) are required. Maliki — one strike for the face and the hands to the wrists is required; a second strike up to the elbows is recommended.
What counts as earth: Hanafi — anything of the earth's kind (dust, sand, stone, lime). Maliki — even stone and snow. Shafi'i and Hanbali — dust only.
Prayers per tayammum: Hanafi — until it breaks, like wudu. Shafi'i and Hanbali — a fresh tayammum for each obligatory prayer (Hanbali: until the time of the prayer ends). Maliki — a fresh tayammum for each obligatory prayer.
Intention: required in all four schools for tayammum.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Allah did not make the prayer depend on water: where water is lacking, earth takes its place, so that no one is shut out of the prayer.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 341 and 343 are the Prophet's ﷺ own lesson to Ammar; the Qur'an verses are 4:43 and 5:6.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Making tayammum when water is available and not harmful; believing it needs a special stone or a two-strike method; praying with it after water has been found.

title: Wiping Over Socks — Masah on the Khuffayn
subtitle: A mercy for cold feet and long journeys
steps: What it is: instead of washing the feet in wudu, you wipe over leather socks (khuffs) or thick socks. The Prophet ﷺ did this and the Companions reported it (Bukhari 202, 203, 204).
The condition: you put the socks on while in a state of wudu. Al-Mughira went to remove the Prophet's ﷺ socks and he said, leave them, I put them on while pure, and wiped over them (Bukhari 206).
How: wet the hands and wipe the top of the socks, from the toes towards the ankle, once. Do not wipe the soles.
How long: for a resident one day and night; for a traveller three days and nights (Muslim 276, Ali). The period begins at the first wiping after the wudu has broken.

What ends it: the end of the period, taking the socks off, or anything that requires ghusl (janabah) — for ghusl the socks must come off. A break in wudu only requires wudu again (wiping over the socks once more within the period).
Wipe over a turban as well as the socks: the Prophet ﷺ did (Bukhari 205). Whether other coverings count is a point on which scholars differ; ask.
sources: The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Duration: Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali — one day and night for a resident, three for a traveller. Maliki — the relied-upon view sets no time limit (the sunnah is to remove the socks once a week).
How: Hanafi — the top of the socks with three fingers. Shafi'i, Hanbali and Maliki — the top, with the bottom also wiped in the Shafi'i and Maliki schools as a sunnah.
Cloth socks: Hanbali, and Hanafi (the position the fatwa follows), allow thick cloth socks that stay on without being tied; the Shafi'i and Maliki schools require leather, or cloth with leather soles. Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: A concession that spares you cold water and a long wash; the Prophet ﷺ made it part of the sunnah.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 202-206 and Muslim 276 are the reports on which every school builds.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Putting the socks on before wudu; wiping the soles; counting the days from putting on the socks instead of from the first wiping.

title: Menstruation & Post-Natal Bleeding — Prayer, Fasting & Qur'an
subtitle: What stops, what continues, what is made up, and where the schools differ
steps: Allah says: 'They ask you about menstruation. Say, it is harm, so keep away from wives during menstruation. And do not approach them until they are pure. And when they have purified themselves, then come to them from where Allah has ordained for you' (Qur'an 2:222). The Prophet ﷺ said: do everything except intercourse (Muslim 302).

Prayer: a woman does not pray while she is menstruating and does not make up those prayers afterwards. When asked, Aisha said: we menstruated in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; we were commanded to make up the fasts and were not commanded to make up the prayers (Muslim 335; Nasa'i 2318, sahih per al-Albani, hasan per Zubair Ali Zai; Bukhari 321).

Fasting: she does not fast while menstruating (Bukhari 304) and makes up the days she missed after Ramadan (Muslim 335; Nasa'i 2318, sahih per al-Albani). If the bleeding starts even just before sunset her fast of that day is invalid, and she makes it up.

When the bleeding stops, she takes a full bath (ghusl) and prays; the Prophet ﷺ said to Fatimah bint Abi Hubaysh: when your menses come, leave the prayer, and when they end, wash the blood off and pray (Bukhari 228, 306). See the ghusl guide.
Tawaf of the Ka'bah is not performed while menstruating; the Prophet ﷺ told Aisha, who began her menses on the way to Hajj, to do everything the pilgrims do except tawaf (Bukhari 294).

The Qur'an and the mosque: the schools differ on touching the mushaf, reciting, and entering the mosque; see the note. Aisha reported that the Prophet ﷺ used to recline in her lap and recite the Qur'an while she was menstruating (Bukhari 297), and he asked her to bring the mat from the mosque, saying your menstruation is not in your hand (Muslim 298).

Irregular bleeding (istihadah): bleeding that is not the monthly period does not stop the prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said to Fatimah bint Abi Hubaysh, who bled continuously: no, it is a blood vessel and not menses (Bukhari 228). She leaves the prayer for her usual days of menses, then bathes, and prays; scholars add that she makes wudu for each prayer (Bukhari 228).

Post-natal bleeding (nifas): Umm Salamah said a woman with post-natal bleeding would wait forty days in the time of the Prophet ﷺ (Abu Dawud 311, hasan sahih per al-Albani and hasan per Zubair Ali Zai; Tirmidhi 139, hasan sahih per al-Albani, hasan per Zubair Ali Zai). If it ends earlier, she bathes and prays. The same rulings on prayer, fasting and tawaf apply as for menstruation.
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 311 (hasan sahih per al-Albani)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Length of the monthly period: Hanafi — at least 3 days and nights, at most 10. Maliki — no minimum; at most 15 days. Shafi'i — at least a day and a night, at most 15 days. Hanbali — at least a day and a night, at most 15 days.
Length of post-natal bleeding: Hanafi and Hanbali — at most 40 days. Maliki and Shafi'i — at most 60 days. There is no minimum in the four schools.
Intimacy: Hanbali — only intercourse is forbidden (Muslim 302). Hanafi, Maliki and Shafi'i — also avoid direct contact between the navel and the knees.
Reciting the Qur'an: Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali — not permitted (dhikr and supplications that are verses, said as dhikr, are allowed). Maliki — permitted. Ibn Taymiyya and some later scholars permit it, as no sound text forbids it; the report that forbids it (Tirmidhi 131) is da'if per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai.
Touching the mushaf: not permitted in the four schools (they cite Qur'an 56:79).
The mosque: Hanafi and Maliki — not permitted to enter. Shafi'i and Hanbali — passing through is permitted, staying is not.
Becoming pure: she is pure when the bleeding has completely stopped; the schools differ on whether she must see a clear white discharge or complete dryness.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: These rulings are a mercy: the woman is excused from prayer and fasting while her body goes through this, and nothing in the rulings makes her unclean as a person.
goDeeper.evidence: Each ruling is from the cited hadith or from the schools' usual positions; the differences are listed in the note.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Making up missed prayers; fasting while bleeding; assuming irregular bleeding stops the prayer; forgetting that the make-up days of fasting remain owed.

title: The Adhan & Iqamah
subtitle: The call that empties the unseen world of devils
steps: The mu'adhin faces the qiblah and raises his voice. The wording the Prophet ﷺ taught Abu Mahdhurah: Allahu Akbar (4 times); Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah (2); Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan Rasulullah (2); then the two testimonies again, repeated (the tarji'); Hayya 'alas-salah (2); Hayya 'alal-falah (2); Allahu Akbar (2); La ilaha illa Allah (Abu Dawud 504, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai; Nasa'i 633, sahih per al-Albani, hasan per Zubair Ali Zai). Muslim 379 gives the same wording. Bilal's adhan, without the repeated testimonies, is the other practice; see the note.
In the Fajr adhan, after Hayya 'alal-falah, add As-salatu khayrun minan-nawm (2) (Abu Dawud 504, sahih per al-Albani; Nasa'i 633, sahih per al-Albani).
Bilal was ordered to say the words of the adhan twice each and the iqamah once, except Qad qamatis-salah, which is said twice (Bukhari 603, 605, 607).
Answer the mu'adhin. Say what he says; at Hayya 'alas-salah and Hayya 'alal-falah say La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah (Muslim 385).

After the adhan send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, then ask Allah to give him the wasilah, the rank in Paradise: whoever asks for it, my intercession becomes due for him (Muslim 384). The Prophet ﷺ taught the supplication Allahumma rabba hadhihid-da'watit-tammah, was-salatil-qa'imah, ati Muhammadanil-wasilata wal-fadilah, wab'athhu maqamam mahmudanil-ladhi wa'adtah, and said that whoever says it after the adhan, my intercession will be due for him on the Day of Resurrection (Bukhari 614).
Supplicate between the adhan and the iqamah: the supplication made between them is not rejected (Abu Dawud 521, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).
Do not leave the mosque after the adhan without a need: Abu Hurayrah said of a man who walked out after the call that he had disobeyed Abu al-Qasim ﷺ (Muslim 655).
The effect of the adhan: Shaytan runs away, passing wind, so as not to hear it; when it ends he returns, and runs away again at the iqamah (Bukhari 608; Muslim 389).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 504 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai), 521 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
Sunan an-Nasa'i 633 (sahih per al-Albani; hasan per Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Form of the adhan: Hanafi and Hanbali — 15 phrases, without the repeated testimonies (Bilal's adhan, as in Bukhari 603). Shafi'i — 19 phrases, with the repeated testimonies (Abu Mahdhurah). Maliki — with the repeated testimonies, and the opening Allahu Akbar said twice, not four times.
Form of the iqamah: Hanafi — every phrase twice (17 phrases), with Qad qamatis-salah twice. Shafi'i and Hanbali — 11 phrases: single phrases except the takbirs and Qad qamatis-salah, which are twice. Maliki — 10 phrases, with Qad qamatis-salah once.
Ruling: Hanbali — a collective obligation (fard kifayah) for the people of a town. Hanafi — a strongly emphasised sunnah. Shafi'i and Maliki — a sunnah that is collective (sunnah kifayah).
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The adhan announces the time, calls people to the prayer and declares the testimony of faith aloud five times a day over a town.
goDeeper.evidence: The wording and the replies above are from Muslim, Bukhari, Abu Dawud and Nasa'i; the numbers are in Sources.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Answering Hayya 'alas-salah with the same words instead of La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah; leaving the mosque after the call.

title: Friday Prayer — The Essentials
subtitle: Jumu'ah: the weekly gathering with conditions and sunnahs
steps: The command: 'O you who have believed, when [the adhan] is called for the prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade' (Qur'an 62:9). After the prayer: 'disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah' (Qur'an 62:10).

Who it is required of: the Prophet ﷺ said the Friday prayer in congregation is a duty on every Muslim except four: a slave, a woman, a boy and a sick person (Abu Dawud 1067, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai). The schools also excuse the traveller; see the note.

Prepare: the Prophet ﷺ said whoever comes to the Friday prayer should bathe (Bukhari 877), and mentioned cleaning the teeth with the siwak and using perfume if available (Bukhari 880); whoever bathes, purifies himself, uses oil or perfume, goes without separating two people sitting together, prays what is written for him and stays silent during the khutbah is forgiven what lies between that Friday and the last (Bukhari 883). See the ghusl guide for the ruling on the bath.
Go early. The Prophet ﷺ compared those who come in the first hour to one who offers a camel, then a cow, a ram, a chicken, an egg (Bukhari 881).

The khutbah: the imam gives two sermons standing, sitting briefly between them (Bukhari 920). Listen in silence: even saying 'be quiet' to your neighbour while the imam speaks is idle talk (Bukhari 934). If you come in while the imam is speaking, pray two short rak'ahs before sitting (Muslim 875, Abu Dawud 1116; sahih per al-Albani); the schools differ on this, see the note.

The prayer: two rak'ahs, led by the imam after the khutbah, complete and not shortened (Ibn Majah 1064, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai). Its time is after the sun has passed its peak (Bukhari 904; Muslim 860). If you miss it, pray Dhuhr.
After the prayer the Prophet ﷺ did not pray in the mosque; he prayed two rak'ahs at home (Bukhari 937).
Send many blessings on the Prophet ﷺ on Friday: he said that the blessings are presented to him (Abu Dawud 1047, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if).

There is an hour on Friday in which a Muslim who asks Allah for something while praying is given it (Bukhari 935). One report places it between the imam sitting down and the end of the prayer (Muslim 853); another, in the last hour after Asr (Abu Dawud 1048, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1047 (sahih per al-Albani), 1048 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai), 1067 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai), 1116 (sahih per al-Albani)
Sunan Ibn Majah 1064 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Who must attend: in all four schools the woman, the traveller, the sick, the slave and the child are excused.
Where and how many: Hanafi — in a city or large town, with the imam and at least three men. Maliki — in a settled community with a mosque, with about twelve men (the relied-upon view). Shafi'i and Hanbali — forty resident adult men (the relied-upon view); a Hanbali narration is three.
Time: Hanafi, Maliki and Shafi'i — after the sun passes its peak. Hanbali — from the time of the Duha prayer, though after the peak is better.
Greeting prayer during the khutbah: Shafi'i and Hanbali — pray two short rak'ahs (Muslim 875). Hanafi and Maliki — sit and listen without praying.
Missed Jumu'ah: pray Dhuhr in all four schools.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Jumu'ah gathers the Muslims of a place every week to hear the reminder and pray together.
goDeeper.evidence: The hadith numbers above were read against the hadith text; the Qur'an verses are quoted from the Saheeh International translation bundled in the app.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Talking during the khutbah; stepping over people's necks; arriving after the khutbah and believing the Friday prayer is valid; forgetting that the traveller and the woman may pray Dhuhr.

title: Eid — The Prayer and Its Etiquette
subtitle: Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha: how the day goes
steps: The two Eids are the Muslims' days of celebration. Fasting on either day is forbidden: Umar said the Prophet ﷺ forbade fasting on the day you break your fast and the day you eat from your sacrifices (Bukhari 1990). The days of Tashriq (11th-13th Dhul-Hijjah) are days of eating and drinking (Muslim 1141).

Wash, wear your best clothes and go to the prayer ground (musalla). On Eid al-Fitr the Prophet ﷺ did not go out until he had eaten some dates, an odd number (Bukhari 953). On Eid al-Adha the schools say to delay eating until after the prayer, so that the first food is from the sacrifice.
The prayer is two rak'ahs, with no adhan and no iqamah, and the khutbah comes after the prayer (Muslim 885, 886; Bukhari 960; Ibn Majah 1064, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).

The takbirs: Aisha reported that the Prophet ﷺ would say the takbir seven times in the first rak'ah and five times in the second on the day of Fitr and the day of Adha (Abu Dawud 1149, sahih per al-Albani, hasan per Zubair Ali Zai). The schools differ on the number; see the note.
What he recited: Surah Qaf in one rak'ah and Surah al-Qamar (54) in the other (Muslim 891).
The khutbah follows; the people sit and listen (Bukhari 956). The Prophet ﷺ went to the women afterwards and exhorted them (Muslim 885).

Everyone comes out, including women: Umm Atiyyah said they were ordered to bring out the girls in seclusion and the menstruating women, who stay behind the men and say the takbir and make dua, and the menstruating women keep away from the prayer place (Bukhari 971, 974).

The takbir of Eid: Allah says: 'to complete the period and to glorify Allah for that to which He has guided you' (Qur'an 2:185), and for Adha, 'remember Allah during [specific] numbered days' (Qur'an 2:203). The wording most Muslims use is Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illallah, wallahu akbar, Allahu akbar wa lillahil-hamd; the Prophet ﷺ is not reported with a single fixed wording in the reports read for this guide, and the Arabic is not added here until it has been checked against a source.

The greeting 'Taqabbal Allahu minna wa minkum' (may Allah accept it from us and from you) is reported from the Companions; this app has not checked the number or the chain of that report, so treat it as a custom, not a command.
Zakat al-Fitr must be paid before the prayer (see the Zakat al-Fitr guide). Eid al-Adha: the sacrifice follows the prayer (see the Udhiyah guide).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1149 (sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai: hasan)
Sunan Ibn Majah 1064 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Ruling of the Eid prayer: Hanafi — wajib. Hanbali — a collective obligation (fard kifayah). Shafi'i and Maliki — an emphasised sunnah.
Extra takbirs: Hanafi — three extra takbirs in each rak'ah (before the recitation in the first, after it in the second). Maliki and Hanbali — six in the first rak'ah and five in the second, besides the opening takbir and the takbir of rising. Shafi'i — seven in the first and five in the second, besides those.
Women and the Eid prayer: Hanafi — no longer encouraged to attend (the later Hanafi position); the other schools — they are encouraged to attend (Bukhari 971).
The prayer ground: Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — it may be prayed in the mosque; the sunnah is the open prayer ground.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Eid is gratitude made visible: fasting ends, the community prays together in the open, and everyone eats.
goDeeper.evidence: The numbers for the prayer and the takbirs are from Muslim, Bukhari and Abu Dawud as listed.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Fasting on Eid; missing the zakat al-Fitr deadline; treating the greeting as obligatory; praying a sunnah before the Eid prayer at the prayer ground.

title: Udhiyah — The Eid al-Adha Sacrifice
subtitle: Who offers it, which animals, when, and how it is shared
steps: What it is: the sacrifice of an animal (sheep, goat, cow or camel) on Eid al-Adha in the name of Allah. Allah says: 'So pray to your Lord and sacrifice [to Him alone]' (Qur'an 108:2). 'Their meat will not reach Allah, nor will their blood, but what reaches Him is piety from you' (Qur'an 22:37).

When: after the Eid prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said: the first thing we do on this day is pray, then return and slaughter; whoever does this has followed our sunnah, and whoever slaughtered before the prayer, it is only meat he gave to his family (Bukhari 5545, 968). Whoever slaughtered before the prayer must slaughter again (Bukhari 5549). The schools differ on how many days; see the note.
The animal's age: the Prophet ﷺ said: sacrifice only a grown animal (musinnah), unless that is difficult for you, then a ram of less than a year but over six months (Muslim 1963).

The animal's condition: it is not permissible to sacrifice an animal with a clearly bad eye, one clearly lame, one clearly sick, or one so emaciated that it has no marrow (Nasa'i 4371, sahih per al-Albani, hasan per Zubair Ali Zai).
Before slaughtering: whoever intends to sacrifice should not cut his hair or nails after the month of Dhul-Hijjah begins until he has sacrificed (Muslim 1977).

How to slaughter: Shaddad ibn Aws reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: Allah has prescribed excellence in everything; so when you kill, kill well, and when you slaughter, slaughter well; let one of you sharpen his knife and let the animal die comfortably (Muslim 1955; Abu Dawud 2815, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai). Say Bismillah, Allahu akbar (Abu Dawud 2810, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if).
Shares: a camel or a cow for seven people (Muslim 1318). Allah says to eat from the sacrifice and feed the needy and the beggar (Qur'an 22:36).

The meat: eat from it, give to relatives and neighbours, and give to the poor. The Prophet ﷺ once forbade keeping the meat beyond three days, then allowed keeping it as long as you like (Muslim 1977). The skin is not sold: the Prophet ﷺ ordered Ali to give the meat, skins and coverings of his sacrificial animals in charity (Bukhari 1718).

One animal for a household: Abu Ayyub said that in the time of the Prophet ﷺ a man would sacrifice a sheep for himself and his family; they ate from it and fed others (Tirmidhi 1505, sahih per al-Albani, isnad hasan per Zubair Ali Zai).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 2810 (sahih per al-Albani; da'if per Zubair Ali Zai), 2815 (sahih per al-Albani)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Ruling: Hanafi — obligatory (wajib) on a resident who owns the nisab. Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — a strongly emphasised sunnah.
Days: Hanafi, Maliki and Hanbali — the day of Eid and the next two days. Shafi'i — the day of Eid and all three days of Tashriq (until sunset on the 13th).
Age: camel five years; cow two years (Maliki: three); goat one year (Shafi'i: two); sheep one year (Hanbali: six months; the Hanafi school accepts a six-month sheep that looks a year old).
Shares: a cow or camel may be shared by up to seven people in the four schools. A sheep or goat is one person's sacrifice; the Maliki school accepts it for the household he supports (Tirmidhi 1505, sahih per al-Albani).
Cutting hair and nails after the new moon of Dhul-Hijjah by one who intends to sacrifice: Hanbali — forbidden. Shafi'i and Maliki — disliked. Hanafi — permitted.
Selling the skin or paying the butcher from the meat: not permitted in any school.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Udhiyah recalls Ibrahim's obedience; what reaches Allah is the piety of the one who sacrifices.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 5545 and Muslim 1963 are the sources for the timing and the age; the Nasa'i report in the sources gives the defects.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Slaughtering before the Eid prayer; selling any part; sharpening the knife in front of the animal; cutting the hair in the first days of Dhul-Hijjah by someone who intends to sacrifice.

title: Making Up Missed Prayers
subtitle: Qada' — the debt that only you can pay
steps: The duty: a missed obligatory prayer is still owed. When the Prophet ﷺ and his companions slept through Fajr on a journey, he said: there is no omission in sleeping; the omission is that a person does not pray until the time of the next prayer comes. Whoever does that should pray when he becomes aware of it (Muslim 681).
Pray it as soon as you remember: the Prophet ﷺ said whoever forgets a prayer should pray it when he remembers it, and there is no expiation for it except that (Bukhari 597; Muslim 684).
Order: the schools differ on whether the missed prayers must be prayed in the order they were missed; see the note.
A missed prayer is made up as the same prayer, with the same number of rak'ahs; a missed Dhuhr is prayed as four rak'ahs.

If you owe many prayers (for example, from years when you did not pray), make an honest estimate of the number, pray the missed prayers alongside your daily prayers until the count is cleared, and ask forgiveness for the neglect. The method is advice from the scholars, not a hadith.

If you missed prayers deliberately: the four schools say they are still owed and must be prayed, together with repentance. A minority of earlier and later scholars (including Ibn Hazm and Ibn Taymiyya in one of his views) held that a prayer deliberately delayed beyond its time cannot be made up, and that repentance and voluntary prayer are the remedy. The majority position is to pray them.
A woman does not make up prayers missed during menstruation or post-natal bleeding (see that guide).
sources: The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Order: Hanafi — order is required, except when the missed prayers reach six or more, or when one forgets, or when the time of the current prayer is too short. Maliki — order is required for a small number (up to four) of missed prayers. Shafi'i — order is recommended, not required. Hanbali — order is required, except for forgetfulness or lack of time.
Praying a current prayer before the missed one: Hanafi, Maliki and Hanbali — the missed prayer comes first when order is required and the time allows. Shafi'i — the current prayer may come first.
Deliberate neglect: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — the prayers are owed and must be made up.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: A prayer owed to Allah is a debt; the Prophet ﷺ did not drop it for someone who slept or forgot.
goDeeper.evidence: Muslim 681 is the account of the night journey on which the Prophet ﷺ slept through Fajr.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Waiting until a convenient time; believing that praying the voluntary prayers replaces the obligatory; delaying until the count feels too large to begin.

title: The Rawatib — Prayers Around the Obligatory
subtitle: The sunnah prayers that guard the fard
steps: The twelve: Umm Habibah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said whoever prays twelve rak'ahs in a day and night, a house is built for him in Paradise: four before Dhuhr, two after it, two after Maghrib, two after Isha and two before Fajr (Tirmidhi 415, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai; Muslim 728 gives the promise without the list).
Fajr: the two rak'ahs before Fajr are dearer to the Prophet ﷺ than the whole world (Muslim 725).

Dhuhr: four before and two after. Umm Habibah also reported that whoever keeps four before Dhuhr and four after it, Allah makes him forbidden to the Fire (Tirmidhi 428, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai). The schools differ on how many are emphasised; see the note.
Asr: the Prophet ﷺ said, may Allah have mercy on a man who prays four rak'ahs before Asr (Abu Dawud 1271, hasan per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai: isnad hasan).

Maghrib and Isha: two rak'ahs after each. Ibn Umar said he remembered ten rak'ahs from the Prophet ﷺ: two before Dhuhr, two after it, two after Maghrib, two after Isha and two before Fajr (Bukhari 1180).

The night prayer: the Prophet ﷺ said it is two rak'ahs and two rak'ahs, and that whoever fears the dawn should pray one rak'ah as witr (Bukhari 990); and that witr should be the last prayer of the night (Bukhari 998). See the witr guide.
Duha: the Prophet ﷺ said the prayer of the penitent is when the young camels feel the heat of the sun (Muslim 748).

Pray the rawatib at home when you can: the Prophet ﷺ said the best prayer of a person is the one he prays in his house, except the obligatory prayer (Bukhari 731), and he prayed his two after Maghrib and Isha at home (Bukhari 1180).
sources: Sunan al-Tirmidhi 415 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai), 428 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
The emphasised sunnahs (sunan mu'akkadah): Hanafi — twelve: two before Fajr, four before and two after Dhuhr, two after Maghrib, two after Isha. Shafi'i — ten: two before Fajr, two before and two after Dhuhr, two after Maghrib, two after Isha. Hanbali — ten (the same as the Shafi'i list). Maliki — only the two before Fajr are strongly emphasised; the others are recommended (mandub).
Asr: the four before are recommended, not emphasised, in the Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools.
If the iqamah begins and you have not prayed the Fajr sunnah: the Prophet ﷺ said that when the prayer commences there is no prayer but the obligatory one (Muslim 710). Shafi'i and Hanbali — join the congregation and make up the sunnah afterwards. Hanafi — pray it first, outside the prayer area, if you will still catch the congregation.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The rawatib are the voluntary prayers that surround the obligatory ones; they repair what is lacking in the fard.
goDeeper.evidence: The list of twelve is in the sources; Muslim 728 gives the same reward and Bukhari 1180 the ten.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Counting the four after Dhuhr as part of the twelve (the list gives two); treating the sunnah as obligatory; skipping the two of Fajr.

title: Mosque Manners
subtitle: The adab of the house of Allah
steps: Enter with the right foot and ask Allah to open the doors of His mercy: the Prophet ﷺ said that when any of you enters the mosque he should say: O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy; and when he leaves, say: O Allah, I ask You for Your bounty (Muslim 713). The Prophet ﷺ liked to begin with the right in all that he did (Bukhari 168); scholars apply this to entering the mosque, and the left foot to leaving.
Pray two rak'ahs before sitting: the Prophet ﷺ said when one of you enters the mosque he should pray two rak'ahs before he sits (Bukhari 444).

Keep your voice low. The Prophet ﷺ heard people reciting aloud in the mosque and said: every one of you is speaking privately to his Lord; do not disturb one another, and do not raise your voice in reciting (Abu Dawud 1332, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).

Do not pass in front of someone praying. The Prophet ﷺ said that if the one who passes in front of a praying person knew the magnitude of his sin, he would rather wait forty (Bukhari 510); and that the one praying should stop anyone who tries to pass between him and his sutra (Bukhari 509).

The mosque is not for trade or announcing lost property. The Prophet ﷺ forbade buying and selling in the mosque and announcing lost things there (Abu Dawud 1079, hasan per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai); whoever hears a man announcing a lost item in the mosque should say, may Allah not return it to you, for the mosques were not built for this (Muslim 568).
Keep it clean of smells: the Prophet ﷺ said whoever eats garlic or onion should keep away from our mosque or stay in his house (Bukhari 855).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1079 (hasan per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai), 1332 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
The greeting prayer (tahiyyat al-masjid): a sunnah in all four schools; the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools emphasise it, the Maliki school calls it recommended. It is not offered at the forbidden times in the Hanafi school.
A woman in menstruation or a person in janabah entering the mosque: Hanafi and Maliki — not permitted; Shafi'i and Hanbali — passing through is permitted, staying is not (see the menstruation guide).
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The mosque is where Muslims gather for prayer; its manners protect the worship of those inside.
goDeeper.evidence: Muslim 713 gives the entering and leaving supplication; the other reports are from Bukhari and Abu Dawud.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Sitting down without the two rak'ahs; talking loudly or using the phone aloud; walking in front of someone praying; coming with the smell of raw onion or garlic.

title: Entering & Leaving the Home
subtitle: Bismillah at the door, gratitude at the threshold
steps: Enter with the right foot (the Prophet ﷺ liked to begin with the right in all that he did: Bukhari 168) and mention Allah's name: when a person enters his house and mentions Allah at the time of entering and at the time of eating, Shaytan says, you have no place to spend the night and no supper (Muslim 2018).
Greet the people of the house: 'when you enter houses, give greetings of peace upon each other — a greeting from Allah, blessed and good' (Qur'an 24:61).

A longer supplication on entering and leaving is reported from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari: O Allah, I ask You for the good of entering and the good of leaving; in the name of Allah we enter, in the name of Allah we leave, and upon our Lord we rely (Abu Dawud 5096). Al-Albani, Abdul Hamid and Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if, so it is not presented here as established.

When leaving, say: Bismillah, tawakkaltu 'alallah, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah. It will be said to him: you are guided, defended and protected, and the devils will go far from him (Abu Dawud 5095, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai: hasan; Tirmidhi 3426, sahih per al-Albani, isnad hasan per Zubair Ali Zai).

Spread the salam inside: the Prophet ﷺ said you will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another; shall I tell you something which, if you do it, will make you love one another? Spread the salam among yourselves (Muslim 54).
Mention Allah's name over food and drink, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is nearest to you (Bukhari 5376).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 5095 (sahih per al-Albani), 5096 (da'if per al-Albani, Abdul Hamid and Zubair Ali Zai)

goDeeper.why: The threshold is where the day outside meets the home; a few words there set the tone for both.
goDeeper.evidence: Muslim 2018 and the Abu Dawud report in the sources give the two phrases; the longer dua is cited as weak, not as a practice.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Treating the weak longer dua as established; forgetting the salam inside the home.

title: Washing & Shrouding the Deceased
subtitle: Ghusl al-mayyit and the kafan — the final service, done gently
steps: Washing, shrouding, praying over and burying a Muslim are a collective duty (fard kifayah): if some people do them, the rest are free of the duty.

The Prophet ﷺ told the women washing his daughter: wash her three times, or five, or more if you see fit, with water and lotus leaves (sidr), and put camphor in the last wash; then inform me (Bukhari 1253, 1254, 1263; Abu Dawud 3142, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).
Begin with the right side and the places of wudu (Bukhari 1255).
Her hair was braided into three plaits and let fall behind her (Bukhari 1263). The Prophet ﷺ gave his waist-wrapper to shroud her (Bukhari 1263).
The shroud: the Prophet ﷺ himself was shrouded in three white cotton sheets, with neither a shirt nor a turban (Bukhari 1264). For a woman, scholars add more pieces; the schools differ, see the note.

Who washes: men wash men and women wash women. A spouse may wash the other in the Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools; see the note. Aisha said that if she had known beforehand what she later knew, none but his wives would have washed the Prophet ﷺ (Abu Dawud 3141, hasan per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai). The Prophet ﷺ also said to her that if she died first, he would wash her, shroud her, pray over her and bury her (Ibn Majah 1465, hasan per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if).
A person who dies in ihram is washed with water and sidr and shrouded in two pieces, without perfume and with the head uncovered; he will be resurrected saying the talbiyah (Bukhari 1265).

The martyr killed in battle is neither washed nor prayed over: the Prophet ﷺ ordered the martyrs of Uhud buried with their blood on their bodies (Bukhari 1343); the schools differ on the prayer, see the note.
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 3141 (hasan per al-Albani), 3142 (sahih per al-Albani)
Sunan Ibn Majah 1465 (hasan per al-Albani; da'if per Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
The shroud: Hanafi — three pieces for a man, five for a woman. Maliki — an odd number, three for a man being sufficient. Shafi'i — three wraps for a man, five pieces for a woman. Hanbali — three wraps for a man, five pieces for a woman.
A spouse washing the other: Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — either spouse may wash the other. Hanafi — the wife may wash her husband, but the husband may not wash his wife.
The martyr of battle: all four schools — not washed. Prayer over him: Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali — not prayed over (Bukhari 1343); Hanafi — prayed over.
Washing as a duty: all four schools — a collective obligation.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The washing and shrouding are the last acts of care that the living give to one who has passed.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 1253-1255 and 1263 give the washing; Bukhari 1264 gives the shroud.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Doing the washing without knowing the steps (ask a trained person or a mosque); omitting camphor in the last wash; uncovering the body unnecessarily.

title: The Funeral Prayer
subtitle: Salat al-janazah — no ruku', no sujud, only dua
steps: The ruling: the funeral prayer is a collective duty (fard kifayah) for the Muslims who are present. The Prophet ﷺ announced the death of the Negus (an-Najashi), took the people out to the prayer ground and prayed over him with four takbirs (Bukhari 1245; Muslim 951).

Stand in rows facing the qiblah. The Prophet ﷺ stood at the middle of the body of a woman who had died in childbirth (Bukhari 1331). The schools differ on where the imam stands for a man; see the note.
First takbir, then al-Fatihah: Ibn Abbas recited it in a funeral prayer and said it is the sunnah (Bukhari 1335). The schools differ here, see the note.
Second takbir, then blessings on the Prophet ﷺ (the same salawat as in the tashahhud).

Third takbir, then the supplication for the dead. Two reports: Awf ibn Malik reported that the Prophet ﷺ prayed over a dead person: O Allah, forgive him, have mercy on him, give him peace and absolve him; receive him with honour and make his grave spacious; wash him with water, snow and hail... (Muslim 963). And Abu Hurayrah reported the prayer: O Allah, forgive those of us who are living and those who are dead, those present and those absent, our young and our old, our male and our female... (Abu Dawud 3201, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai: isnad hasan; Tirmidhi 1024, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).
Fourth takbir, a short pause, then the salam. Zayd ibn Arqam usually said four takbirs but once said five, and reported that the Prophet ﷺ had said five (Muslim 957).

The reward: whoever attends the funeral until he prays over it has a qirat; whoever stays until the burial has two qirats, like two great mountains (Bukhari 1325). And if forty men who associate nothing with Allah pray over a Muslim, Allah accepts their intercession for him (Muslim 948).
If the body is not present (a prayer in absentia, as for the Negus): see the note.
sources: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1024 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Al-Fatihah: Shafi'i and Hanbali — required after the first takbir. Hanafi — the opening supplication (thana') and praise, not al-Fatihah (unless as a supplication). Maliki — no al-Fatihah (the relied-upon view); supplication only.
Where the imam stands: Hanafi — at the chest of the body, man or woman. Maliki — at the middle of a man and the shoulders of a woman. Shafi'i — at the head of a man and the middle of a woman. Hanbali — at the chest of a man and the middle of a woman.
The salam: Hanafi and Shafi'i — two salams. Maliki — one. Hanbali — one is required, a second is recommended.
Prayer in absentia (salat al-ghaib): Shafi'i and Hanbali — permitted. Hanafi and Maliki — not permitted.
Number of takbirs: four in the four schools.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The funeral prayer is made of supplication: its whole purpose is to ask Allah's forgiveness and mercy for the one who has died.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 1245 and Muslim 951 give the four takbirs; Muslim 963 and the Abu Dawud report in the sources give the supplications.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Praying with ruku' or sujud; forgetting that the wording of the supplication changes for a child or a woman (ask a teacher); leaving before the prayer when the rows are forming.

title: The Burial & Visiting Graves
subtitle: Hasten the burial; visit to remember, not to worship
steps: Hasten it: the Prophet ﷺ said, hurry with the dead body: if it was righteous, you are forwarding it to good; and if otherwise, you are putting an evil down from your necks (Bukhari 1315).

Placing him in the grave, the Prophet ﷺ said: Bismillah wa 'ala sunnati Rasulillah, in the name of Allah and on the sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (Abu Dawud 3213, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai; Tirmidhi 1046, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).
The body is laid on its right side facing the qiblah, in a niche (lahd) where the ground allows; the schools agree on this practice, and no sound text is cited here for the detail.

Scatter earth: the Prophet ﷺ scattered three handfuls of earth from the head side of the grave (Ibn Majah 1565, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if). Some scholars add the words of Qur'an 20:55, 'From the earth We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will extract you another time'; the narration for saying it is weak.

After the burial: the Prophet ﷺ used to stay at the grave and say, seek forgiveness for your brother and ask steadfastness for him, for he is being questioned now (Abu Dawud 3221, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai: isnad hasan).
Do not build over graves, plaster them or sit on them: Jabir reported that the Prophet ﷺ forbade it (Muslim 970).

No wailing: the Prophet ﷺ said whoever slaps his cheeks, tears his clothes and follows the ways of the Days of Ignorance is not one of us (Bukhari 1294). Crying is mercy: the Prophet ﷺ wept at the death of his son Ibrahim and said, the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord (Bukhari 1303).

Visiting graves: the Prophet ﷺ said, I forbade you to visit graves, but now you may visit them (Muslim 977); visit the graves, for they remind you of the Hereafter (Ibn Majah 1569, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).

The greeting: Buraydah reported that the Prophet ﷺ taught them to say on going to the graveyard: peace be upon you, people of this place, among the believers and the Muslims, and God willing we shall join you; I ask Allah for safety for us and for you (Muslim 975). Aisha was taught a similar greeting (Muslim 974).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 3213 (sahih per al-Albani), 3221 (sahih per al-Albani)
Sunan Ibn Majah 1565 (sahih per al-Albani; da'if per Zubair Ali Zai), 1569 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Women visiting graves: Hanafi — permitted. Maliki — permitted for older women, disliked for young women. Shafi'i and Hanbali — disliked. The Prophet ﷺ cursed women who visit graves in one report (Tirmidhi 1056, hasan per al-Albani); scholars differ on whether it was abrogated.
Lahd or shaqq: all four schools prefer the niche (lahd) where the ground allows.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Burial is quick, simple and carried out by the living for the dead; the visit to graves keeps the Hereafter in mind.
goDeeper.evidence: Each ruling above is from the cited hadith; the scholars' differences are in the note.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Delaying the burial for convenience; raising a loud wail; building over a grave; asking the dead for help instead of asking Allah for the dead.

title: Consoling the Bereaved
subtitle: What to say when there is nothing to say
steps: The words of the believer in affliction: Allah says: 'Who, when disaster strikes them, say, Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return' (Qur'an 2:156). The Prophet ﷺ taught that whoever says it and adds, O Allah, reward me for my affliction and give me something better than it in exchange, Allah will give him something better (Muslim 918).

What the Prophet ﷺ sent to console his daughter: whatever Allah takes is His, and whatever He gives is His, and everything has a fixed term with Him; so be patient and hope for Allah's reward (Bukhari 1284). These are words of condolence taught by the Prophet ﷺ.

Crying is allowed; the Prophet ﷺ wept and said: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord (Bukhari 1303). Slapping the cheeks and tearing clothes are forbidden (Bukhari 1294).
Serve the family: bring food. The Prophet ﷺ said, prepare food for the family of Jafar, for something has come upon them that keeps them busy (Abu Dawud 3132, hasan per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).

How long mourning lasts: Umm Habibah said she heard the Prophet ﷺ say it is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn a dead person for more than three days, except for a husband, for whom the period is four months and ten days (Bukhari 1280).
Keep praying for the dead: when a person dies, his deeds end except three: continuing charity, knowledge that benefits others, or a righteous child who prays for him (Muslim 1631).
A report that whoever consoles a bereaved person has the same reward as him (Tirmidhi 1073) is da'if per al-Albani, Ahmad Shakir and Zubair Ali Zai, so it is not given as a promise.

goDeeper.why: Condolence is for the living: it steadies the bereaved and reminds them that Allah is the One who gives and takes.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 1284 gives the Prophet's own words of condolence; Muslim 918 gives the du'a of the bereaved.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Saying 'it was his time' coldly; telling someone not to cry; forgetting the family afterwards, when the visitors have gone.

title: Eating Manners
subtitle: Bismillah, the right hand, moderation, and thanks
steps: Begin with Bismillah. The Prophet ﷺ said, when one of you eats he should mention Allah's name, and if he forgets at the beginning he should say 'Bismillahi awwalahu wa akhirahu' (in the name of Allah at the beginning and at the end of it) (Abu Dawud 3767, sahih per al-Albani).

Eat with the right hand and eat from what is nearest. He said to a boy whose hand roamed the dish, 'O boy, mention the name of Allah, eat with your right hand and eat from what is nearest to you' (Bukhari 5376). He said that Satan eats with his left hand and drinks with his left hand (Muslim 2020).

Do not fill the stomach. He said, 'A human being fills no worse vessel than his stomach. It is sufficient for him to eat a few mouthfuls to keep his spine straight. But if he must, then one third for food, one third for drink and one third for air' (Ibn Majah 3349, sahih per al-Albani).
Eat together. He said, 'The food for two is sufficient for three, and the food of three is sufficient for four' (Bukhari 5392).

Thank Allah while you eat. He said, 'Allah is pleased with His servant who says Al-hamdu lillah when he takes a morsel of food and when he drinks' (Muslim 2734). When the dining sheet was taken away he used to say 'Al-hamdu lillahi kathiran tayyiban mubarakan fihi, ghayra makfiyyin wa la muwadda'in wa la mustaghnan 'anhu, Rabbana' (Bukhari 5458).

Keep food clean and good. Allah says, 'O you who have believed, eat from the good things which We have provided for you and be grateful to Allah if it is [indeed] Him that you worship' (Qur'an 2:172). What counts as halal and haram food is in the Halal Food guide.

goDeeper.why: Eating is an act that Allah has made a means of worship when it begins with His name and ends with His praise.
goDeeper.evidence: Each manner above is a quoted hadith; the wording of the closing dua is from Bukhari 5458.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Eating until full as a habit; eating with the left hand without need; forgetting Bismillah and not saying the dua for forgetting.

title: Halal Food — What Is Lawful and What Is Not
subtitle: The Qur’an's list, the hadith additions, and where the schools differ
steps: The default: 'O mankind, eat from whatever is on earth [that is] lawful and good and do not follow the footsteps of Satan' (Qur'an 2:168).

The Qur'an's list of what is forbidden to eat: 'dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah' (Qur'an 2:173; 5:3). Surah al-Ma'idah adds animals killed by strangling, a violent blow, a fall or the goring of horns, and what a wild animal has eaten, 'except what you [are able to] slaughter [before its death]' (Qur'an 5:3).

Added by the hadith: the Prophet ﷺ forbade the eating of the meat of beasts having fangs (Bukhari 5530); in another narration, every fanged beast of prey and every bird having talons (Muslim 1934). On the day of Khaybar he ordered the pots of domestic donkey meat to be emptied (Bukhari 5497).

Intoxicants: 'intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it' (Qur'an 5:90). He said, 'Every intoxicant is khamr and every intoxicant is forbidden' (Muslim 2003).
The sea: 'Lawful to you is game from the sea and its food as provision for you' (Qur'an 5:96). He said of the sea, 'Its water is pure and its dead is lawful' (Abu Dawud 83, sahih per al-Albani).

Slaughter: 'do not eat of that upon which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed, it is grave disobedience' (Qur'an 6:121). The Prophet slaughtered with his own hands, saying Bismillah and Allahu Akbar (Bukhari 5558). Meat of the People of the Scripture: 'the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you' (Qur'an 5:5).
Necessity: whoever is forced 'neither desiring [it] nor transgressing [its limit], there is no sin upon him' (Qur'an 2:173).

Doubtful things: the Prophet ﷺ said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters that most people do not know; whoever avoids the doubtful has protected his religion and honor (Bukhari 52). Read ingredient labels; ask when you cannot tell.
sources: The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Sea animals: Hanafi — only fish; other sea animals are disliked or forbidden (scholars differ about shrimp). Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali — sea animals are generally lawful; a few exceptions are named in each school (for example, frogs).
