'Those who spend their wealth [in Allah's way] by night and by day, secretly and publicly - they will have their reward with their Lord' (Qur'an 2:274).

The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah will give shade on the Day when there is no shade but His to seven, among them 'a man who gives charity so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right hand has given' (Bukhari 660).

Even a little. 'Save yourselves from the Fire even with half a date, and if this is not available, then by a good word' (Bukhari 6023). He said, 'Sadaqa is due on every joint of a person every day the sun rises... a good word is a sadaqa, and every step you take towards prayer is a sadaqa, and removing harmful things from the path is a sadaqa' (Muslim 1009).

Lawful earnings. He said, 'If one gives in charity what equals one date from honestly earned money, and Allah accepts only the honestly earned, Allah takes it in His right hand and enlarges its reward' (Bukhari 1410).

It does not decrease wealth. He said, 'Charity does not decrease wealth' (Muslim 2588). Every day two angels come down: one says 'O Allah, compensate every person who spends', the other, 'O Allah, destroy every miser' (Bukhari 1442).
madhhabNote: Voluntary charity (sadaqah) has no fixed amount or time, unlike zakat. The schools agree on this; the details of what may be given from zakat and what only from sadaqah are in the Zakat guide.

goDeeper.why: Voluntary giving is the sign of a heart that is not attached to wealth.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 660 and Qur'an 2:271 on hiding the gift; Muslim 1009 on forms of sadaqah beyond money.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Giving for show; thinking only large gifts count; reproaching the one you gave to.

title: A Daily Portion of Qur'an
subtitle: Reciting every day, with understanding and measure
steps: Keep it regular. The Prophet ﷺ said, 'The most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant, even if it were little' (Bukhari 6464).

Reward. He said, 'Whoever recites a letter from Allah's Book gets a reward, and the reward is ten times its like' (Tirmidhi 2910, sahih per al-Albani). 'The one who is proficient in the Qur'an is with the noble, upright recording angels, and the one who falters in it and finds it difficult has two rewards' (Muslim 798).

Pace. 'And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation' (Qur'an 73:4). He told Abdullah ibn Amr to finish it in a month, then in fewer days, and the last advice was seven days (Abu Dawud 1388, sahih per al-Albani). He said, 'He who recites the Qur'an in less than three days does not understand it' (Abu Dawud 1394, sahih per al-Albani).
Begin with refuge. 'So when you recite the Qur'an, [first] seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the expelled [from His mercy]' (Qur'an 16:98).
Learn it and teach it. 'The best among you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it' (Bukhari 5027).
Do not abandon it. 'And the Messenger has said, "O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as [a thing] abandoned"' (Qur'an 25:30).

Purity and the mushaf: 'None touch it except the purified' (Qur'an 56:79). Most scholars use this and other evidence to require wudu to touch the printed mushaf; see the note. Reciting from memory without wudu is permitted.
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1388 (sahih per al-Albani), 1394 (sahih per al-Albani)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Touching the mushaf: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali — wudu is required for touching it. Some scholars, including the Zahiri school, hold it is not required. Whether Qur'an 56:79 refers to the mushaf or to the angels is itself discussed.
Reciting while in major impurity (janabah): the majority hold it is not permitted; some scholars allow a verse or two for protection. Menstruating women: see the Menstruation guide.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The Qur'an is meant to be recited, understood and acted upon each day.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 6464 gives the principle of regularity; the rest of the guide quotes the texts on reward, pace and purity.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Reciting rarely and in bulk; neglecting to understand; touching the mushaf without wudu without knowing the school's view.

title: Teaching Your Children the Deen
subtitle: Luqman's advice, the prayer at seven and ten, and mercy
steps: Begin with tawhid. Luqman said to his son: 'O my son, do not associate [anything] with Allah. Indeed, association [with him] is great injustice' (Qur'an 31:13).

Luqman's advice then: 'O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you' (Qur'an 31:17); 'do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people and do not walk through the earth exultantly' (31:18); 'be moderate in your pace and lower your voice' (31:19).

Protect your family. 'O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire' (Qur'an 66:6). The Prophet ﷺ said, 'Every one of you is a guardian and is responsible for his charges... a man is a guardian of his family and is responsible for them' (Bukhari 2554).

The prayer. He said, 'Command your children to pray when they become seven years old, and beat them for it when they become ten, and arrange their beds separately' (Abu Dawud 495, hasan sahih per al-Albani). Scholars who accept the wording limit the blow to a light one that does not injure, and many teachers use no striking at all.

Mercy. Al-Aqra' said he had ten children and had never kissed any; the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Whoever is not merciful to others will not be treated mercifully' (Bukhari 5997). He also said, 'He is not one of us who does not have mercy on our young' (Tirmidhi 1919, sahih per al-Albani; Abu Dawud 4943, sahih per al-Albani).
Make dua for them. Ibrahim said, 'My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [many] from my descendants' (Qur'an 14:40).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 495 (hasan sahih per al-Albani), 4943 (sahih per al-Albani)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
A child is not obliged to pray until puberty. Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali — the guardian commands prayer at seven and the child may be disciplined for neglecting it at ten, in the manner described above. The details of discipline are for a scholar and, in many countries, the law.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Teaching children is a trust: begin with tawhid, then prayer, character and mercy.

title: Tahajjud — The Night Prayer
subtitle: What the Qur’an, Bukhari and Muslim say about praying in the night
steps: What it is: a prayer of the night. The Qur’an uses its verb: “And from [part of] the night, pray with it as additional [worship] for you; it is expected that your Lord will resurrect you to a praised station.” (Qur’an 17:79).

The Qur’an praises those who rise for it. Of the righteous: “They arise from [their] beds; they supplicate their Lord in fear and aspiration” (Qur’an 32:16), and “They used to sleep but little of the night, And in the hours before dawn they would ask forgiveness” (Qur’an 51:17-18). Surah al-Muzzammil opens by telling the one wrapped in his clothing: “Arise [to pray] the night, except for a little” (Qur’an 73:2), and goes on to speak of half of it, a little less or a little more, with measured recitation (Qur’an 73:3-4).

The last third: Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said our Lord descends each night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and calls: who will call on Me so I answer, ask Me so I give, seek My forgiveness so I forgive (Sahih al-Bukhari 1145; Sahih Muslim 758). How this is understood is a matter for scholars of belief; this guide only reports the hadith.

In pairs: a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about the night prayer and he said it is prayed two rak’ahs at a time; whoever fears the dawn prays one rak’ah, which makes what he prayed odd (Sahih al-Bukhari 990, from Ibn Umar).

Begin with two short rak’ahs: Aisha reported that when the Prophet ﷺ rose to pray at night he began with two short rak’ahs (Sahih Muslim 767), and Abu Hurayrah reported that he advised whoever rises for the night prayer to begin with two short rak’ahs (Sahih Muslim 768).

How many: Aisha was asked about his night prayer and said he did not go beyond eleven rak’ahs in Ramadan or in other months: four, then four, then three (Sahih al-Bukhari 1147). That is her report. The sources used here do not set a number you must pray, and this guide does not state how the schools count it: ask a teacher.
Close it with witr: Ibn Umar reported the Prophet ﷺ said to make the witr your last prayer at night (Sahih al-Bukhari 998). The Witr and night guide has the qunut and the dua.
Its weight: Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said “the most excellent prayer after what is prescribed is prayer during the night” (Sahih Muslim 1163).

What this guide does not say: whether tahajjud has to follow sleep, a fixed rak’ah count, or how each school ranks these points. The sources it cites do not settle them here. Prayer Times shows tonight’s window for the last third of the night.

title: What Is Islam?
subtitle: The word, the verses and the hadith, in plain order
steps: The word: Islam is usually translated “surrender” or “submission” to God (Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Islam”). The Qur’an uses the same Arabic root in “to Him have submitted [all] those within the heavens and earth, willingly or by compulsion” (Qur’an 3:83) and in the words of the believers: “we are Muslims [submitting] to Him” (Qur’an 3:84).

In one line, put together from the sources in this guide (not a scholar’s definition): Islam is submission to Allah alone, worshipping Him and following the guidance He sent through His messengers, the last of whom is Muhammad ﷺ.

What the Qur’an says of it: “Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.” (Qur’an 3:19). And: “And whoever desires other than Islam as religion - never will it be accepted from him, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers.” (Qur’an 3:85). And of Muhammad ﷺ: “the Messenger of Allah and last of the prophets” (Qur’an 33:40).

The five pillars (Ibn Umar reported the Prophet ﷺ said Islam is built on five): the testimony that none deserves worship but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger, the prayer, zakat, the pilgrimage, and fasting Ramadan (Sahih al-Bukhari 8).

Islam, iman and ihsan: in the hadith of Jibril, Umar reported that the Prophet ﷺ described Islam as those pillars; iman as belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day and the divine decree; and ihsan as worshipping Allah as though you see Him (Sahih Muslim 8).
Where to go next: the New Muslim path in this app takes one short step a day, and the Aqeedah school teaches what Muslims believe. For a person, ask a local imam or a teacher you trust.

title: The Four Schools — How They Differ
subtitle: What a madhhab is, and one worked example with its sources
steps: What a madhhab is: a school of thought within Islamic jurisprudence (Wikipedia, “Madhhab”). The four Sunni schools are the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi’i and the Hanbali, each named after a classical jurist. This guide does not rank them and does not give a ruling.

The example: the hands in standing prayer. Sahl ibn Sa’d reported that people were told to place the right hand on the left forearm in prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari 740). Where exactly on the body is where scholars differ.

Hanafi: below the navel. Shafi’i: above the navel (Dorar adds: and below the chest). Both are stated by the Dorar al-Saniyya fiqh encyclopedia (dorar.net/en/feqhia/76) and by Sheikh Ahmad Kutty of the Islamic Institute of Toronto (fiqh.islamonline.net, “The position of hands in prayer”).

Maliki and Hanbali: the two sources above do not give one fixed placement. Sheikh Ahmad Kutty says some Maliki scholars hold the hands at the sides, and that reports from Imam Ahmad give both below and above the navel. Dorar says that for Imam Ahmad the choice is broad. Read these as what those sources say, not as the schools’ final word.

What they agree on: Sheikh Ahmad Kutty writes that all scholars agree the prayer is valid with the hands above the navel, below it or on the chest, and that Tirmidhi and Ibn al-Mundhir noted both placements among the Companions and their successors.

Other differences are marked in their own guides: the qunut in the Witr and night guide, Ramadan Nights, Fasting, Making Up Missed Prayers, Ghusl and the Hajj guides each carry a note on where the schools differ.
The Huda guides’ own rule: follow one school’s fiqh completely, or ask a local teacher. For your own case, ask a qualified scholar of your school.
